In multiple enclosures housing black-and-white ruffed lemurs and red ruffed lemurs, there are areas of excessive rust. On
the metal bars that make up the frame of the enclosures, there are sections where the metal has rusted through. This has
created holes with rough, rusted edges that compromise the surface of the bars and are in places where the lemurs can
access it.
Rust can compromise structural strength, present roughened or broken surfaces where it is possible for the nonhuman
primates to injure themselves, and prevent proper cleaning and sanitization of a surface. Any surfaces that come in
contact with the nonhuman primates must be free of excessive rust that prevents the required cleaning and sanitization,
or that affects the structural strength of the surface.
To be corrected by July 14, 2026.

The facility was not providing potable water as often as necessary for five red ruffed lemurs. In the enclosure housing two
adult red ruffed lemurs and three juvenile red ruffed lemurs, both water bowls were empty and dry. When the attending
veterinarian provided water in one of the bowls, the inspector observed that both adults immediately went to the water and
drank continuously for almost one and half minutes. Both adults briefly moved away but returned to the bowl and drank
water for an additional minute.
Inadequate access to potable water can cause distress and dehydration of the animals. Potable water must be provided
in sufficient quantity to every nonhuman primate housed at the facility. If potable water is not continually available to the
nonhuman primates, it must be offered to them as often as necessary to ensure their health and well-being, but no less
than twice daily for at least 1 hour each time, unless otherwise required by the attending veterinarian.
To be corrected by end of day on June 23, 2026.
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the attending veterinarian and facility representatives.
